clue.text: Seize forger in such a coat

blocks.note: to claw at something is to seize it
a smith forges metal with this tool, so it is a forger

explanation.surface: A criminal is arrested while wearing a particular style of coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forger' looks like a criminal, but here it is the tool that forges metal on an anvil.
explanation.definitionFit: A claw-hammer coat is a formal tailcoat, named because its split tails resemble the claw end of the tool.

clue.text: The start of Housman's heavenly beacon

definitions.text: The start of Housman's heavenly beacon

blocks.clueFragment: The start of Housman's heavenly beacon
blocks.note: surface reading: where a signal fire begins its blaze in a poem
setter's reading: the hill named as the place where the beacon starts in A Shropshire Lad

explanation.walkthrough: A Shropshire Lad opens 'From Clee to heaven the beacon burns'; the beacon fires begin on the Clee Hills of Shropshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The Clee Hills in Shropshire are where Housman's poem has the jubilee bonfire lit, the starting point of the heavenward blaze.

clue.text: A mistake over a string for David's hot-water bottle

blocks.note: taken as written
bish is British slang for a blunder
taken as written
G is a string on a violin or guitar

explanation.surface: A musician's slip on one string, said to be meant for King David the harpist.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' simply puts the first pieces above the rest. Bish is old British slang for a mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: In 1 Kings the young woman Abishag was brought to lie with the aged King David and keep him warm.

clue.text: Jolly giddy this, said Kipling

blocks.note: surface reading: someone cheerful and dizzy
setter's reading: a Jolly is a Royal Marine, whom Kipling's poem calls a giddy something, being soldier and sailor too

explanation.walkthrough: In Kipling's 'Soldier an' Sailor Too' the Marine is 'a kind of a giddy harumfrodite'. Jolly is old navy slang for a Royal Marine.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's soldier's mispronunciation of hermaphrodite describes the Marine as both soldier and sailor, combining two natures in one person.

clue.text: Mother taken poorly holds father up - don't take this literally

indicators.note: something taken poorly is out of sorts, so the word's letters are disordered
to hold something is to keep it within, so one piece goes inside the other
in a down clue, going up means reading the word from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
pa is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: A sick mother clutching her husband, with a warning not to read it at face value.
explanation.definitionFit: A metaphor describes one thing in terms of another, so its words are figurative rather than meant literally.

clue.text: Epic poet in the middle of Greece

indicators.note: only the central letters of the next word are kept
one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: Alexander Pope, the poet who translated Homer's epics
the two central letters of this six-letter word

explanation.surface: A poet of epics stands at the heart of Greece, as Homer did.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Epic poet' reads as one phrase, Homer perhaps; the definition is only 'Epic'.
explanation.definitionFit: An epopee is an epic poem, from the Greek for the making of epic verse.

clue.text: Stage whisper to disconcert

indicators.note: a whisper is something spoken, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a stage is a phase of a process

explanation.surface: An actor's stage whisper meant to unsettle someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage whisper' looks like the theatrical phrase; it splits into a word and the signal to say it.
explanation.definitionFit: To faze someone is to disturb or fluster them, the same as to disconcert them.

clue.text: Give naughty girl, going topless, a little air

indicators.note: losing the top means the first letter is dropped from the name

blocks.note: Naughty Marietta is Victor Herbert's 1910 operetta

explanation.surface: A cheeky suggestion to give a wayward girl who strips off some fresh air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naughty girl' points to the title heroine of Naughty Marietta; 'a little air' sounds like ventilation but is a short tune.
explanation.definitionFit: An arietta is a short aria, the diminutive of the Italian word for an operatic song or melody.

clue.text: Cretan teacher comes to Eastern divines by about mid-March

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for Eastern
pious men: PI is the crossword abbreviation for pious, plus MEN
the Ides of March fell on the fifteenth, about the middle of the month

explanation.surface: A Cretan teacher meets Eastern clergy around the middle of March.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divines' are clergymen, read as pious men; 'by' just places one piece beside the next.
explanation.definitionFit: Epimenides was a semi-legendary philosopher and seer from Crete, famous for the paradox that all Cretans are liars.

clue.text: A measure for the study of defamation in quitting one's country

indicators.note: one thing given for another means it takes that other's place in a longer word

blocks.note: an em is a printer's measure of width
a den is a private study or retreat
denigrating someone is defaming them

explanation.surface: Someone researching libel decides to leave the country.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the word for defamation and swap its opening study for the printer's measure.
explanation.definitionFit: Emigration is the act of leaving one's native land to settle abroad, the noun for quitting a country.

clue.text: Save, classically, from an agonising fate

indicators.note: the letters are taken out from within the following words

blocks.note: the letters sit inside this word
surface padding: it completes the picture of a grim end and gives no letters

explanation.surface: A plea to be rescued from a painful end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Save' reads as a verb meaning rescue; here it is the preposition meaning except, in Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: Nisi is Latin for unless or except, and save can mean except, as in 'all save one'.

clue.text: Sort of pill that helped produce a born sneerer

definitions.text: Sort of pill that helped produce a born sneerer

blocks.note: surface reading: a medicine tablet with odd side effects
setter's reading: Pooh-Bah in The Mikado traces his ancestry to a primordial globule and so was born sneering

explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert's Pooh-Bah says he can trace his ancestry back to a primordial atomic globule, and so was born sneering. A globule is a pill.
explanation.definitionFit: Pooh-Bah's ancestral globule is described in that very line by this adjective, meaning of the primitive living substance in cells.

clue.text: Ayesha married the brother of young Peggotty's namesake

definitions.text: the brother of young Peggotty's namesake

blocks.note: Ayesha is She-who-must-be-obeyed in Rider Haggard's novel She
M is the abbreviation for married

explanation.surface: A heroine weds the brother of a Dickens character's namesake.
explanation.walkthrough: Young Peggotty in David Copperfield is Ham, named like Noah's son, whose brothers were Shem and Japheth.
explanation.definitionFit: Ham Peggotty shares a name with Noah's son Ham, and Shem was one of that biblical Ham's brothers.

clue.text: The Woman in White working overseas, perhaps

definitions.text: The Woman in White working overseas, perhaps

blocks.note: surface reading: Wilkie Collins's heroine, apparently employed abroad
setter's reading: a female clown in white costume performing on a seaside pier, which stands over the sea

explanation.walkthrough: Pierrot troupes in white costume were a staple of British seaside piers, so 'overseas' means literally above the water.
explanation.definitionFit: A pierrette is the female counterpart of Pierrot, the white-faced clown in loose white costume of pantomime and seaside shows.

clue.text: In which Washington had his share of the whim-whams

definitions.text: In which Washington had his share of the whim-whams

blocks.clueFragment: Washington had his share of the whim-whams
blocks.note: surface reading: George Washington suffering a bout of the jitters

blocks.clueFragment: In which Washington had his share
blocks.note: setter's reading: the periodical Washington Irving co-wrote, subtitled the Whim-Whams and Opinions of Launcelot Langstaff

explanation.walkthrough: Washington is Washington Irving, not the president; his 1807 periodical with his brother and James Paulding carried 'whim-whams' in its subtitle.
explanation.definitionFit: Irving's periodical took its title from a dish of chopped meat and anchovies, a word also meaning a miscellany or mixture.

clue.text: Lived in Half-Moon Street and had a brother in Worthing

definitions.text: Lived in Half-Moon Street and had a brother in Worthing

blocks.note: surface reading: a Mayfair resident with family in a Sussex seaside town
setter's reading: Wilde's young man in The Importance of Being Earnest, who turns out to be Jack Worthing's brother

explanation.walkthrough: Worthing reads as the Sussex resort but is Jack Worthing, revealed at the end of Wilde's play to be the brother of his friend from Half Moon Street.
explanation.definitionFit: Algernon Moncrieff keeps rooms in Half Moon Street and discovers that Jack Worthing is his elder brother.

clue.text: Artist's production of “The Clouds"

indicators.note: a production makes something new out of material, so these letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A painter's staging of Aristophanes' comedy The Clouds.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks suggest the Greek play; the definition is plain clouds of one kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Strati is the plural of stratus, the low flat grey sheet of cloud, so it names a set of clouds.

clue.text: Tragedian in “The Vortex” wanting a proportionate rise

indicators.note: a vortex is a whirl, so the letters caught in it are spun into a new order
wanting means lacking, so the named letter is taken out

blocks.note: taken as written
the letter to be removed

explanation.surface: An actor playing in Noël Coward's The Vortex seeks a fair pay rise.
explanation.walkthrough: The Vortex was Noël Coward's 1924 play; the title doubles as the signal to stir the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A gradient is a slope measured as the ratio of height gained to distance travelled, a rise in proportion.

clue.text: Facts reflected in state of Zaire

definitions.note: the definition is a place belonging to Zaire, a Zairean port

indicators.note: a reflection shows things back to front, so the word reads backwards
one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: data are facts
MI is the postal abbreviation for Michigan

explanation.surface: Information mirrored in the government of the African state of Zaire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State of Zaire' reads as one phrase; the state is an American one, and the answer is a place of Zaire.
explanation.definitionFit: Matadi is the chief seaport of Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, on the Congo River.

clue.text: Doctrine in which most of the love is between Frenchmen

indicators.note: most but not all, so the final letter is cut
a piece placed between others sits inside them

blocks.note: taken as written
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
MM is the abbreviation for Messieurs
taken as written

explanation.surface: A creed in which love chiefly passes between Frenchmen.
explanation.walkthrough: MM, Messieurs, is the French plural of Mr, so it splits round the middle piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomism is the philosophical and theological system of St Thomas Aquinas, a body of doctrine of the Catholic Church.

clue.text: No need to take a bath first when picture-making with this

definitions.text: No need to take a bath first when picture-making with this

blocks.clueFragment: No need to take a bath first
blocks.note: surface reading: someone excused from washing before painting
setter's reading: a photographic plate that was coated ready for use, unlike the old wet process dipped in a silver bath just before exposure

explanation.walkthrough: Wet collodion plates had to be sensitised in a silver nitrate bath immediately before exposure; the gelatin type replaced them in the 1870s.
explanation.definitionFit: A dry plate is a glass photographic plate coated with gelatin emulsion that could be prepared and stored long before use.

clue.text: Italian intensifier, for example, fitted in S African missile

indicators.note: something fitted in is placed inside another piece

blocks.note: assai is Italian for very, used in musical directions
e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia

explanation.surface: An Italian word of emphasis set inside a South African weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: Assai appears in tempo markings such as allegro assai, very fast.
explanation.definitionFit: An assegai is a slender iron-tipped spear thrown or thrust by Zulu and other southern African warriors.

clue.text: Left to skulk outside, Milton's horrid king

indicators.note: one piece goes around the outside of the other

blocks.note: to mooch is to loiter or slink about
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: An abandoned figure lurks outside the dwelling of Milton's terrible king.
explanation.walkthrough: Paradise Lost introduces him as 'Moloch, horrid king, besmeared with blood'.
explanation.definitionFit: Moloch is the Canaanite god of child sacrifice whom Milton names among the fallen angels as a horrid king.

clue.text: Tweed's one example of a spirit message

blocks.note: a ghost is a spirit
word can mean news or a message

explanation.surface: A medium relays a message from a ghost about the River Tweed.
explanation.walkthrough: Tweed, the cloth, is said to come from a clerk misreading tweel, the Scots form of twill.
explanation.definitionFit: A ghost word is a word born from a scribal or printing error, and tweed is often cited as arising from misread tweel.

clue.text: Russell admits writing under signature for church feature

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: AE was the pen name of the Irish poet George William Russell
a postscript is added below where a letter is signed

explanation.surface: Someone named Russell lets in a note written below his signature.
explanation.walkthrough: Russell looks like a philosopher; he is the Irish poet who signed himself AE.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the semicircular vaulted recess at the east end of a church, an architectural feature of the building.

clue.text: Disheartened like a goose girl

indicators.note: losing the heart means the central letters of the word are removed

blocks.note: anserine means of or like a goose, from Latin anser

explanation.surface: A dispirited, silly girl who minds the geese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goose girl' reads as one phrase from the fairy tale; the definition is only 'girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne is a common female forename, so it serves as an example of a girl's name.

clue.text: It ran through both temples in Canaan

definitions.text: It ran through both temples in Canaan

blocks.clueFragment: ran through both temples in Canaan
blocks.note: surface reading: something passing through two shrines of the Holy Land
setter's reading: the spike Jael drove through Sisera's head, the temples being the sides of the forehead

explanation.walkthrough: In Judges 4, Jael killed the Canaanite general Sisera by driving a tent peg through his temple into the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Older Bibles call Jael's tent peg by this word, the spike she hammered through the sleeping general's skull.

clue.text: Sides of ham have each gone bad, coming from Holland

indicators.note: the sides of a word are its first and last letters
something gone bad is spoilt, so its letters are disordered

blocks.note: the opening side of this word
taken as written, the first of its two uses
the closing side of this word
taken as written again, since each side gets a copy

explanation.surface: Both ends of a ham have spoilt, the meat having been imported from Holland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Each' means each side gets its own scrambled copy of the word. Hogen-mogen, from Dutch hoogmogend, was an old English nickname for the Dutch.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an old English jocular name for the Dutch States-General, from their title High Mightinesses, so it means Dutch.

clue.text: She's back in the City of the Golden Temple

indicators.note: only a run of letters lying in the longer name is kept, the rest dropped
read back means read from right to left

blocks.clueFragment: the City of the Golden Temple
blocks.note: the Golden Temple of the Sikhs is in this Punjab city

explanation.surface: A woman returns to the holy Sikh city in India.
explanation.walkthrough: The hidden letters are inside a city the clue only describes, so the city must be named first.
explanation.definitionFit: Irma is a woman's first name, so it fits a pronoun standing for any particular female.

clue.text: Talk to the Lily Maid — she's the key-holder

blocks.note: to chat is to talk
Elaine the Lily Maid of Astolat, in Tennyson's Idylls of the King

explanation.surface: Go and speak to the fair maiden, as she is the one holding the keys.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson calls Elaine 'the lily maid of Astolat'; she died for love of Lancelot.
explanation.definitionFit: A chatelaine is the mistress of a large house, traditionally carrying its keys on a chain at her waist.
